The post When community colleges close, rural students get shut out of the liberal arts  appeared first on The Hechinger Report.
item.content:encoded:
This story was originally published by Barn Raiser and is reprinted with permission.

Last May, just weeks before the end of the semester, students, staff and faculty at the University of Wisconsin—Platteville Baraboo Sauk County received the devastating news that the school was closing. Students scrambled to arrange transfers to other colleges, while employees tried to line up jobs elsewhere in the UW system. 

By the end of the month, “Boo U,” as it was affectionately named, a fixture in south-central Wisconsin for nearly 60 years, was no more.

The Baraboo campus was just the latest UW school to close its doors. In the past three years, the University of Wisconsin has permanently shuttered eight of its 13 branch campuses. With their focus on the liberal arts, these two-year transfer colleges long provided an accessible, affordable on-ramp to higher education, especially for rural and first-generation college students. 

To mark Boo U’s closing, instructors and students held a celebration to pay tribute to the college. Among the guests: members of the very first graduating class, who received their associate degrees in the 1970s, two years after the school opened.

“It was really a memorial,” says Karen DeSanto, a first-term Wisconsin state legislator who represents Baraboo. “The students talked about how this place shaped and changed lives in this community. We don’t have that any more.”

In recent years the pace of colleges shutting down has ticked up. According to analysis by The Hechinger Report, colleges are now closing at a rate equivalent to nearly one every three weeks. And yet within this trend, the demise of Wisconsin’s two-year public colleges remains something of an outlier. The other colleges that have closed or are at risk of closing are overwhelmingly private institutions.

University of Wisconsin officials have cited steep declines in enrollment to justify the closure of the campuses. While the UW system has seen enrollment drop by more than 10 percent since 2010, the decline has been especially acute at the two-year schools. In its final year of operation, Boo U had just 100 students, down from more than 500 just a decade ago. Plunging student numbers meant that revenue was no longer enough to keep up with facility, staff and infrastructure costs.

But a shortage of students is only part of the story. Years of budget cuts, beginning under former Republican Gov. Scott Walker in 2015, in concert with a series of tuition freezes, have left the UW system among the worst funded in the nation. 

Then in 2017, UW approved a sweeping merger, making the two-year colleges regional branches of the state’s four-year schools. This set off a competitive scramble for students that pitted the two-year UW schools against bigger, and better resourced institutions, some of which lowered admissions requirements to lure more students. 

“At that point the writing was really on the wall,” says Dan Kallgren, who spent his career teaching history at UW-Marinette, outside of Green Bay. 

Marinette ended in-person instruction in 2024, then limped along for another year offering remote classes. Kallgren taught the final course at the school: a Western Civilization survey class, beamed out via video link to students in Manitowoc and Sheboygan. “I was the last faculty member on campus,” recalls Kallgren.

UW officials insist that even with the shuttering of the rural campuses, Wisconsin students still have plenty of options to choose from, including 13 four-year schools across the state and 16 technical colleges. 

But Kallgren says that argument fails to acknowledge the unique role that liberal arts schools like Marinette have played in letting rural students effectively try out college.  

“Think about the rural kid screwing up his courage and coming here, then getting turned on to engineering or history,” says Kallgren. “That avenue is now closed.”

Education deserts

Despite the popular notion of students venturing far away to attend college, most students enroll at a campus within 20 miles of home. That’s according to extensive research by scholar Nicholas Hillman, who formerly directed a research lab at UW-Madison and is now an education professor at Indiana University. Hillman found that proximity to a college is associated with higher levels of postsecondary enrollment. 

But the inverse is also true. As distance grows between a student and a school, the odds of them enrolling drops. Hillman calls regions with fewer colleges and universities “education deserts,” and warns that Wisconsin is pursuing the higher education equivalent of “desertification.”

“They’ve hollowed out the two-year schools and the liberal arts transfer mission and now they’re sealing the coffin,” says Hillman. “The question is, if you shut one door, have you opened another?”

That doors are closing for Wisconsin’s rural students appears to be borne out by data. Previous reporting on college access in rural communities found that the number of rural students enrolled in the UW system has dropped at a rate greater than the overall decrease in college attendance. While the decline has many causes, including a political backlash against higher education in the state’s conservative rural regions, the shuttering of the branch campuses is likely to exacerbate that trend. 

The winnowing of college options in states like Wisconsin reflects a larger story about institutions that serve low-income and rural students closing or being starved of resources. 

“People don’t realize the contrast between schools where programs are being cut and (UW-)Madison where the world is your oyster,” says Douglas Haynes, a professor of English at UW-Oshkosh and the author of “Teaching Toward Slow Hope: Place-Based Learning in College and Beyond,” a new book on higher education in the upper Midwest. “There are going to be increasing numbers of (rural) students who just don’t go to college any more.”

A recent study found that Wisconsin has the second highest rate of “brain drain” in the country, as young, educated workers move out of the state after graduating. Haynes says that diminishing college access creates another form of brain drain in which young rural Wisconsinites are deprived of opportunities at the front end. “When we limit college access we’re also limiting the kind of impact these students might have had in their own communities,” says Haynes.

The Wisconsin Idea

Alex Stevens grew up in Stevenson, Michigan, a small town on the Upper Peninsula. Unlike many of his high school classmates, Stevens always knew that he wanted to attend college, but with a disabled mother, both distance and cost were major concerns. 

“I was raised by my grandparents, and I knew that caring for my mother was going to become my responsibility,” says Stevens. He would end up choosing the nearest college option, 25 miles down the road and over the state line in Wisconsin: UW-Marinette. “It just made sense to go there.”

He thrived at the school with its small campus and intimate class sizes. Stevens’ favorite courses were sweeping interdisciplinary examinations of U.S. history taught by professors of history, music and film. 

After two years, and with almost no college debt, Stevens transferred to UW-Green Bay to pursue a history degree. He now teaches history and social studies at a Catholic high school in Marinette. 

“I was rural, poor, and smart and UWM gave me a remarkable opportunity,” says Stevens.

Today, Stevens’ trajectory is much less likely, and not just because the Marinette campus is gone. Wisconsin has also steadily moved away from the liberal arts emphasis that was at the core of the mission of the two-year transfer schools. 

Homegrown: How Rural Communities Build Their Workforce

Rural America needs workers—but is there enough local education and training to meet the need?  Five nonprofit newsrooms in Wisconsin, North Carolina, West Virginia, Oklahoma and Northern California examine how rural higher education and workforce programs try to fill critical shortages of health care workers, teachers and skilled labor. This collaboration from INN’s Rural News Network explores the promises and missed opportunities to create strong rural workforces. 

In 2023, Jay Rothman, who served as president of the University of Wisconsin before he was fired in April of this year, set off a firestorm with his recommendation that colleges in the system shift from liberal arts programs to more career specific programs, “particularly if the institution serves a large number of low-income students.” 

An investigation by student journalists at UW-Madison found that of 82 academic programs within the UW system that have been cut or eliminated in recent years, the majority were in the humanities or social sciences.

“There is an increasingly narrow focus on vocational education,” says Alyssa Ratledge, who studies rural higher education issues at MDRC, a nonprofit research group. She says that closure of the branch campuses and the elimination of majors reflect a broader shift in how states like Wisconsin view the purpose of higher education.

“It’s all about getting a job with a positive ROI (return-on-investment),” says Ratledge. “But students also go to college to try things out and discover who they are.”

As the branch campuses disappear, the expansive notion of higher-education-for-all known as the Wisconsin Idea — the Progressive-era vision that education should improve people’s lives outside the classroom — is also in retreat. In Baraboo, the community is now debating what to do with a cluster of empty buildings. 

In Marinette, the theater arts program is the only one remaining, thanks to a partnership with UW Green-Bay, private donations and event ticket sales. Lauryn Albaugh is in charge, and she’s hopeful that the programming, including community and children’s theater, will inspire young people here as it did when she was growing up in Marinette. 

Cast in “Willy Wonka Jr.” at the age of 7, Albaugh has never looked back. 

“I really attribute my love for the arts to this theater program,” she says. “That it’s thriving feels very encouraging.”

Still, today Albaugh is one of just two employees left at UW-Marinette — a maintenance man inspects the mothballed facilities once a week. 

Jennifer C. Berkshire is the host of the education podcast “Have You Heard” and the co-author (with Jack Schneider) of The Education Wars: A Citizen’s Guide and Defense Manual. She teaches in the Boston College Prison Education Program and the Education Studies program at Yale. 

This story was originally published by Barn Raiser.

This reporting is part of a collaboration with the Institute for Nonprofit News‘ Rural News Network. Five nonprofit newsrooms were involved: Barn Raiser, Carolina Public Press, Mountain State Spotlight, Oklahoma Watch and Shasta Scout. The series was edited by veteran investigative editor Dee J. Hall, co-founder and former managing editor of Wisconsin Watch. Support from Ascendium Education Group made this project possible.

item.title: 39 meta-analyses, 39 positive findings: An audit finds serious flaws in research on AI in education
item.dc:creator: Jill Barshay
item.description:

The post 39 meta-analyses, 39 positive findings: An audit finds serious flaws in research on AI in education  appeared first on The Hechinger Report.
item.content:encoded:
Does artificial intelligence help students learn? That’s a question many teachers and parents want answered, as the new educational technology is rapidly spreading in classrooms. 

Normally, meta-analyses would be the right place to look, since they’re supposed to gather a scattered body of research and make sense of it by pointing to where the preponderance of evidence lies. And indeed, there are 39 of them, all reporting substantial benefits for AI in education. 

But it appears that the studies synthesizing that evidence are themselves unreliable — and the peer-review process failed to catch the problems. 

“This is not trustworthy evidence,” said Justin Reich, an associate professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and the director of MIT’s Teaching Systems Lab, who hosted a webinar on Oct. 20 to discuss the problem of the growing number of positive AI meta-analyses. “All of these meta-analyses are flawed.”

A forensic audit of 14 of the 39 meta-analyses has found serious conceptual and statistical flaws. Appearing in journals by prominent publishers, including Springer Nature, Wiley, SAGE and Taylor & Francis, these 14 papers have accumulated more than 3,000 citations and continue to rack up 200 citations a month, according to Google Scholar — implying that AI’s effectiveness is settled science. One meta-analysis has been retracted, almost a year after its May 2025 publication in a Nature journal after two Norwegian scholars lodged a complaint. 

The new audit was conducted by Patrick O’Neill, a community college professor at the Bloomington, Indiana, campus of Ivy Tech, who examined a sample of the underlying studies and the statistical methods used to combine their results in meta-analyses. O’Neill found recurring patterns of errors, some of which he said could easily have been detected just by reading the study abstracts. 

During the Oct. 20 webinar, O’Neill described a constellation of “impossible statistics,” “hallucinated references” and “overstated conclusions.” Some of the underlying studies even cited references to papers published about generative AI before that technology was released to the public. Links to the citations sometimes led to unrelated studies. 

Many of the aggregated studies didn’t even measure how much AI boosted learning. For example, nursing students who studied for three hours a week with an instructor using AI were compared to peers who had no study sessions at all (of course they tested better). Students who played video games and answered AI-generated questions outperformed students who did neither. In another experiment, students who chatted with an AI bot reported feeling less anxious.

Beth Tipton, a leading meta-analysis expert and a professor at Northwestern University, who joined her colleagues Reich and O’Neill in the critique, characterized as “crazy” the idea of conducting a very broad meta-analysis encompassing all the various uses of AI in education.  

Tipton compared it to conducting a meta-analysis of math education. Is math education effective? That depends on how the math is taught. A thoughtful meta-analysis might narrow the question down to a specific approach, such as whether spatial learning interventions improve math skills. Similarly, Tipton said, how AI is used needs to be specified before conducting a meta-analysis of it. 

“Do we mean people using [educational] apps and programs that include AI in them, like Khan Academy? Do we mean giving students access to Claude?” Tipton asked. 

A big concern in the current batch of AI meta-analyses, O’Neill said, is “publication bias.” He found that two-thirds of the calls for papers for AI in education specifically invited research on its benefits, “seemingly disinviting null or negative results.” That means the meta-analyses are effectively “manufacturing evidence” by aggregating selected, positive results, he said. 

Recrunching the numbers

O’Neill is now conducting his own AI meta-analysis, using proper statistical methods, and arriving at a far less sanguine picture. He found that the outcomes from 44 well-designed experiments varied widely, from very helpful to very harmful to students. The results averaged out to roughly zero, according to O’Neill’s preliminary calculations. This doesn’t mean educators should conclude that AI is harmless, on average. It depends on how it’s used.

Susanna Loeb, a Stanford professor of education who also joined the meta-analysis critique webinar, pointed out that her team has collected almost 900 studies on AI in education and determined that only 20 of them were of high enough quality to be included in a recent summary of the evidence for her AI Hub for Education. Her team has since identified 32 more studies and is soon to update that summary. But, she said, it’s still too early to conduct a meta-analysis that would be useful to school leaders or teachers. Very few of the high-quality studies take place in K-12 schools in the United States.

Northwestern’s Tipton worries that the fast-growing field of meta-analysis has outstripped the supply of experts qualified to review the work. More scholars are conducting meta-analyses because they’re quicker and cheaper than running experiments, and they can attract lots of citations for ambitious professors. The hunger for evidence about AI has made this topic a particular magnet for meta-analysis and spawned something of an AI meta-analysis cottage industry.

Tipton said she gets requests to review meta-analysis papers every day but can’t accept them all. Checking the underlying studies can take days, and peer review is unpaid volunteer work.

Medicine has flawed research, too, Tipton said, but it has gatekeepers to help separate the wheat from the chaff. The Food and Drug Administration evaluates evidence before approving drugs, and insurers review research when deciding which treatments to cover. Education has no comparable safeguards.

A ‘no-man’s land’

“In education, it’s kind of no-man’s land,” Tipton said. “Anybody can sort of say that they have evidence for anything, and share it with anybody, and consumers, schools, teachers, parents are left to try to wade through that and make sense of it. It’s incredibly frustrating.”

The researchers appealed to philanthropic funders and the National Science Foundation for help supporting rigorous, reliable research syntheses. “Maybe our model of voluntary peer review doesn’t work very well for landmark” studies on critical topics in education, Reich said. “Peer review’s not working. Meta-analysis is not working.”

Until truly reliable evidence emerges, the researchers advised educators to experiment cautiously with AI, starting with small groups of students and monitoring the results. Even introducing AI into a 300-student lecture course could be risky, O’Neill said.

In other words, teachers are on their own to experiment in their own classrooms. Still, it’s encouraging to see education researchers calling out flaws in their own field and trying to fix them.
